title: NIST SP 1800-38C: Quantum Readiness Interoperability and Performance Preliminary Draft — Phase 65 GSA post-quantum acquisition review
publisher: National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, NIST
summary: Phase 65 reviews this primary record as part of the GSA post-quantum acquisition reporting pack. The preliminary practice-guide volume documents controlled, non-production interoperability and performance testing for draft post-quantum implementations across selected protocols and collaborator components.
key_findings: The draft frames interoperability testing as a way to identify and resolve compatibility issues before organizations repeat the same work independently.

The guide records protocol-specific test profiles, collaborator components, algorithm selections, and performance considerations rather than treating post-quantum migration as a single software update.
For the documented QUIC test, only one implementation was available at initial testing, so the team could not complete interoperability testing for that protocol.
why_it_matters: Which records move a migration obligation through inventory, solicitation, award, interoperability test, cutover, acceptance, rollback, and legacy retirement? This record supplies one bounded part of that evidence chain; it is not a substitute for the pack's downstream records. The draft supplies inspectable laboratory evidence beneath broad post-quantum policy, while showing that implementation diversity and protocol maturity are practical migration constraints.
ftfn_relevance: Strengthens Cybersecurity and Quantum with a specific testbed artifact.
Separates algorithm standardization from protocol support, interoperability, performance, product integration, procurement, and institutional migration.
Provides a bounded baseline for tracking later draft and final practice-guide artifacts.
evidence_limits: Inclusion in a Phase 65 reporting pack does not advance a Phase 64 matrix cell or establish an operating outcome.
The document is a preliminary draft whose public-comment period has closed.
Controlled laboratory testing does not prove production interoperability, vendor support, procurement, or completed migration.
Protocol-specific results and implementation availability may be superseded by later standards and software.
